result.summary: The poet invokes Calliope to sing of Helios, child of Hyperion and Euryphaessa, and describes him riding his radiant chariot across the sky. The hymn ends with a farewell, a prayer for sustenance, and a promise to move on to the race of half-divine mortals.

scenes.title: Invocation and Helios's chariot
scenes.summary: The poet asks Calliope to sing of Helios, names his parents and siblings, and describes his shining chariot journey across heaven to Ocean.

scenes.title: Farewell and prayer
scenes.summary: The poet greets Helios, asks for heart-cheering substance, and says he will turn next to the race of half-divine mortals.
scenes.stakes: The poet seeks livelihood and the Muses' favor for his next song.

alias_notes.alias: Son of Earth and starry Heaven
alias_notes.explanation: A periphrasis for Hyperion, a Titan, child of Gaia and Ouranos.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid picture of the sun god's radiant helmet, locks and fluttering garment.

analysis.text: The hymn presents the sun as a divine, watchful charioteer whose daily course links heaven and Ocean, showing the gods' presence in natural order.
Homeric Hymns served as preludes to recitations; the closing promise to turn to mortal heroes reflects this performance use.

legacy.text: The image of the sun god driving a chariot across the sky became a lasting motif in Greek and Roman poetry and art.

fun_facts.text: Calliope is named here as the Muse invoked, and is traditionally the Muse of epic poetry.

language_notes.text: "Bare" is the archaic past tense of "bear": Euryphaessa gave birth to Helios.
"Son of Earth and starry Heaven" is Hyperion, a Titan, child of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Heaven); his name is given in the next sentence.
"Stayed" means halted. Helios pauses at midday at heaven's peak before descending toward Ocean in the west.
"Substance" means livelihood or wealth, here the means of living well, which "cheers the heart."
The "race of mortal men half-divine" refers to the heroes, whose deeds the poet will sing next, as hymns typically lead into other songs.

context_notes.text: Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry, often named chief of the Muses. Hymns commonly open by calling on a Muse.
Eos is the Dawn and Selene the Moon, so Helios the Sun has the other great lights of the sky as siblings.
Ocean is the great river encircling the world in Greek thought; the sun was imagined sinking into it at day's end.

literary_notes.text: Stock descriptions like "rosy-armed," "rich-tressed" and "tireless" give each sibling a fixed identifying trait, in epic style.
Rays, streaming locks and a fluttering garment make the sun's radiance vivid through light and movement.
The poet speaks as a performer, closing the hymn and announcing the next song, as in the conventional transition formula.
